title: Singly linked list assignment problems
overview: This module is solving time: assignment problems that must be done with a singly linked list. Each one mixes the basic moves — build with `insert_at_tail`, walk with a `tmp` pointer, delete by relinking — into a small task: max minus min, search for an index, compare two lists, handle insert/delete queries and remove duplicates. Revising these shows how far the few core operations can take you.

concepts.explain: The input lists end with `-1`. A `while(true)` loop reads a value, `break`s on -1, and otherwise appends it to the list.
concepts.snippet: while(true){ cin >> v; if(v == -1) break; insert_at_tail(head, tail, v); }

concepts.explain: Max, min, size and search all use the same pattern: a `tmp` pointer from `head` to `NULL`, updating a running value (or a running index) at each node.
concepts.snippet: for(Node* t = head; t != NULL; t = t->next) { ... }

concepts.explain: Keep a counter that starts at 0 and goes up by one each time `tmp` moves; when the value matches, the counter is the index.
To compare two lists, check the sizes first, then move `tmp1` and `tmp2` one step at a time and stop at the first different value.
An index is valid only when `0 <= idx < size`. Index 0 is the head case, and when the removed node was the last one, `tail` must be moved back.
For each `outer` node, an `inner` pointer scans the rest of the list and unlinks every later node with the same value. The first occurrence of each value stays, so the order is kept.

files.title: Difference between max and min
files.what: Reads a list and prints the largest value minus the smallest value, found with two separate walks.
steps: Build the list until `-1`.
`find_max` walks the list with `max` starting at `INT_MIN`.
`find_min` walks it again with `min` starting at `INT_MAX`.
Print `max - min`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) for the list

check.q: Could max and min be found in one walk?
check.a: Yes — update both running values inside the same loop.

files.title: Max minus min (practice copy)
files.what: Identical re-typing of the max–min difference solution.
steps: Same two walks for max and min, then subtract.

check.q: What does the program print for a one-value list `9 -1`?
check.a: 0, because max and min are both 9.

files.title: Search: first index of X
files.what: For each test case, builds a list and prints the 0-based index of the first node equal to `X`, or -1 if it is missing.
steps: Read `T`, the number of test cases, and loop `while(T--)`.
Each case starts with a fresh `head`/`tail` and reads values until -1.
Read `X`, then `find_index` walks the list with `index` starting at 0.
Return `index` at the first match; return -1 after the loop if nothing matched.
Print the result on its own line.
files.complexity: Time O(n) per test · Space O(n)
files.input_note: T, then for each test: the list ended by -1, then X on the next line.
files.output_note: `2` (2 is at index 2), `-1` (9 is missing), `0` (the first 4 is at index 0 — the search stops at the first match).

check.q: Why is `head` declared inside the `while(T--)` loop?
check.a: So every test case starts with an empty list instead of adding to the previous one.

files.title: Search for X (practice copy)
files.what: Same solution, but the line that prints the answer is missing.
steps: Same building and `find_index` walk; the result is stored in `index` and never used.
files.complexity: Time O(n) per test · Space O(n)
files.output_note: Empty output — the program computes the answers but never prints them.
files.watch_out: Add `cout << index << endl;` after `int index = find_index(head, X);`.

check.q: What should the three answers be for this input?

files.title: Are two lists exactly the same?
files.what: Reads two lists and prints YES only if they have the same length and the same value at every position.
steps: Build list 1 and list 2, each ended by -1.
`is_similar` first compares `get_size` of both; different sizes → NO.
Then `temp1` and `temp2` move together for `size1` steps.
At the first position where the values differ, print NO and return.
If the loop finishes, print YES.
files.complexity: Time O(n + m) · Space O(n + m)
files.output_note: `YES` — same size and same values in the same order.

check.q: Why check sizes before comparing values?
check.a: Otherwise one pointer could reach `NULL` while the other still has nodes, and reading `->val` from `NULL` crashes.

files.title: Same lists (practice copy)
files.what: Same idea, but the comparison loop runs `while(tmp1 != NULL)` instead of counting to `size1`.
steps: Size check first, then walk both lists until `tmp1` reaches the end.
files.complexity: Time O(n + m) · Space O(n + m)
files.output_note: `NO` — the sizes match but position 1 holds 20 vs 25.

check.a: Yes, because the sizes are already known to be equal, so `tmp2` runs out at the same moment.

files.title: Insert/delete queries
files.what: Starts with an empty list and handles Q queries: `0 V` inserts V at the head, `1 V` inserts V at the tail, `2 V` deletes index V if it is valid. After each query the list is printed.
steps: Read `Q`, then for each query read `X` and `V`.
`X == 0` → `insert_at_head`; `X == 1` → `insert_at_tail` (this version walks to the end each time).
`X == 2` → `delete_at_any_position`, which returns early if the list is empty or `idx >= size`.
Index 0 deletes the head and sets `tail = NULL` if the list became empty.
Otherwise walk to `idx-1`, unlink the next node, and move `tail` back if the last node was removed.
Print the list after every query.
files.complexity: Time O(n) per query · Space O(n)
files.input_note: Q, then Q lines of `X V`.
files.output_note: Lines: `10`, `10 20`, `5 10 20`, `5 20` (index 1 removed), `5 20` (index 7 is invalid, nothing happens), `20` (head removed).
files.watch_out: If the list becomes empty the program prints an empty line — check whether the judge wants that. `insert_at_head` does not update `tail` for later inserts, which is fine only because `insert_at_tail` here walks from the head.

check.q: For a list of size 3, which delete indexes are valid?

files.title: Insert/delete queries (practice copy)
files.what: Same solution, except the validity check is `idx > get_size(head)` instead of `>=`.
steps: Same query handling as the original.
files.complexity: Time O(n) per query · Space O(n)
files.input_note: Q, then Q lines of `X V`.
files.output_note: Same output as the original for this input: `10`, `10 20`, `5 10 20`, `5 20`, `5 20`, `20`.
files.watch_out: Off-by-one: deleting index == size passes the check. For list `10 20`, the query `2 2` walks to the last node, then `tmp->next->next` reads from `NULL` and the program crashes. Use `idx >= get_size(head)`.

check.a: Indexes go from 0 to size−1, so there is no node at index `size`.

files.title: Remove duplicate values
files.what: Deletes every repeated value from the list, keeping the first occurrence of each, then prints the list.
steps: `outer` walks the list one node at a time.
For each `outer`, `inner` starts at `outer` and looks at `inner->next`.
If `inner->next->val` equals `outer->val`, unlink and `delete` that node — and do NOT move `inner`, because the new `inner->next` still needs checking.
Otherwise move `inner` forward.
When `inner` reaches the end, move `outer` forward.
files.output_note: `2 5 3 1` — the later 2 and both later 5s were removed; the order of first occurrences is kept.
files.watch_out: This `insert_at_tail` walks the whole list for every value, so reading input is O(n²) even though `tail` is available. Using `tail->next = newNode` makes it O(1).

check.q: Why does `inner` not move after a deletion?
check.a: Its new `next` is an unchecked node; moving on would skip it and could leave two equal values side by side.

files.title: Remove duplicates (practice copy)
files.what: Same algorithm with the `if` written the other way round (test for equal first, then the else moves `inner`).
steps: Identical two-pointer duplicate removal.

check.q: If the list were sorted, how could duplicates be removed faster?
check.a: Equal values sit next to each other, so a single walk comparing each node with its `next` is enough — O(n).

recap: Most list problems are one walk with a running value: size, max, min, index.
Compare two lists: sizes first, then walk both together.
A valid index satisfies `0 <= idx < size`; watch `>` vs `>=`.
When a delete removes the last node, move `tail` too.

check_yourself.q: Why do the query solutions check `head == NULL` before deleting?
check_yourself.a: An empty list has no node to remove, and walking from a `NULL` head would crash.

check_yourself.q: In duplicate removal, which occurrence of each value is kept?
check_yourself.a: The first one; only later copies are unlinked.

check_yourself.q: What does `find_index` return for a value that appears twice?
check_yourself.a: The index of its first appearance, because it returns as soon as it finds a match.
